reason: The dependence unit is the physical accident event. Form FRA 6180.54 is a per-railroad, per-consist report, and the shipped rows are not strictly one per event: build.py:469-472 makes colliding composite keys (same railroad code, date, state, station, milepost, accident type) unique by appending a sequence suffix, so the uniqueness check at build.py:621-634 passes by construction. Public rows show 7 such suffixed pairs in train and 4 in eval, plus same-date/same-state/same-scene pairs that differ only in consist fields or railroad class. No shipped column identifies the event exactly, because railroad code, station and milepost are hashed into accident_id and then discarded (build.py:106-115,495). accident_date is the finest shipped column that is constant across every report of one event; the contract names it event_key_column and a non-predictor carry (construction.json:4-6,120), and because the split is on this date (build.py:491-493) a cluster can never straddle train, eval and holdout. It is a deliberate coarsening: accident_date plus stateabbr is nested inside it and was not chosen so the key stays valid if two reports of one event disagree on state. Chosen from source meaning, contract metadata and public train/eval structure before holdout scoring; no holdout row or holdout metric was consulted.
limitations: accident_date is a superset of the event, not an event identifier: unrelated accidents on the same day are merged (in train, 6,576 date clusters for 12,541 rows, 3,008 singletons, largest cluster 10 rows). This costs some efficiency, not validity.

Repeated-carrier and repeated-location dependence is not captured. The reporting railroad code, station and milepost are not shipped, and reporting_railroad_class has too few levels (one class holds roughly 80-88% of public rows) to serve as a cluster.

Calendar-level dependence across days (reporting-threshold regimes, the base-rate decline, multi-day weather) is not captured by day clusters; per-year results should be read alongside any clustered interval.
An event whose reports carry different accident dates (midnight straddle or entry error) would be split across clusters. Not checked.

That the paired rows are multiple reports of one accident is an inference from Form 54 meaning and public-row structure; the publisher data dictionary was not consulted and the pairs were not traced to source records.

Holdout cluster-size distribution is unknown because holdout rows were not read. Rows dated by the January 1 fallback (build.py:431-442) would pool into one cluster per year; no such spike appears in train or eval (16 and 11 January 1 rows).

The observed multi-report structure is small (about 0.1-0.2% of public rows), so clustered and row-level intervals are expected to be close; the key is declared for correctness of the independence assumption, not because a large effect is anticipated.
